assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: The Meaning of Failure: Identity, Learning, or Excuse
assets.visual_frame_description: A busy courtroom has just emptied after a verdict. Maya Chen, a 34-year-old attorney, stands alone at the plaintiff's table, six years of case files stacked beside her; her team lost the suit against the bank that their clients said cheated them. On a split screen, three other faces appear in ghosted panels: a football player in a Vikings jersey, a three-star French chef in a kitchen, and a tennis player berating a camera crew. The player sees each figure tagged with a one-line reaction to losing.
assets.player_mission: Read the reaction of each person in the scene and classify which response pattern each one shows: failure treated as a permanent identity, failure treated as an event to learn from, or failure handled by repairing self-esteem through blame or downward comparison. Sort every evidence row into the correct column before advancing.
key_concepts: In the fixed mindset, failure is transformed from an action ("I failed") into an identity ("I am a failure").
Bernard Loiseau, a three-star Michelin chef, was possessed by the idea that a downgrade in a guide had redefined him as a failure and a has-been.
The Martins cooled toward their three-year-old son Robert and stopped treating him with pride after he failed to get into the number one preschool in New York.
Jim Marshall, after running a fumble recovery the wrong way for a touchdown on national television, decided at halftime, "If you make a mistake, you got to make it right."
College students in the fixed mindset, after doing poorly on a test, chose to look at the tests of people who had done really poorly as a way to feel better about themselves.
John McEnroe blamed anything but himself for losses: a fever, a backache, the tabloids, a friend being in love, and an NBC cameraman's headset noise during the 1984 French Open.
John Wooden said you are not a failure until you start to blame, because you can still be learning from your mistakes until you deny them.
Seventh graders with the growth mindset said they would study harder after a poor grade, while those with the fixed mindset said they would study less and would seriously consider cheating.
Jack Welch, after the Kidder, Peabody scandal, phoned fourteen of his top GE colleagues to apologize personally, saying "I blamed myself for the disaster."
In the growth mindset, failure is a painful but nondestructive problem to be faced, dealt with, and learned from.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests how mindsets change the meaning of failure: in the fixed mindset a setback becomes a verdict on fixed identity, while in the growth mindset it is an event to face and learn from. Dweck also shows that fixed-mindset people repair self-esteem after failure through blame, excuses, and downward comparison rather than through repairing the underlying skill.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Maya Chen, highlighted at the plaintiff's table, just lost the six-year case she brought for clients who felt cheated by a bank. Which column best classifies Maya's response to losing?
assets.column_b_label: Failure as an event to learn from (growth mindset)
assets.column_c_label: Self-esteem repair via blame or downward comparison (fixed mindset)

rows.label: Maya tells a colleague, "Who am I to say that just because I spent seven years on something I am entitled to success? I do not regret it. I had to do it."
Jim Marshall pulls himself together at halftime and plays some of his best football, contributing to his team's victory.
John McEnroe explains his 1984 French Open loss to Ivan Lendl by blaming noise from an NBC cameraman's headset.
College students, after failing a test, choose to review the test papers of students who did far worse than they did.
Bernard Loiseau, the three-star chef, becomes possessed by the idea that losing two points in a guide has redefined him as a has-been.
The Martins stop treating three-year-old Robert with pride and affection after he failed to get into the number one preschool.

distractors: Failure as identity: the loss permanently brands Maya as someone who could never win.
Self-esteem repair: Maya is blaming the bank or the judge to protect her ego.
Maya's reaction is best explained by temperament, since sensitive people can never let go of a loss.
assets.explanation: Maya separates the outcome from her worth: she asks whether she fought for success or for the validity of the effort itself, refuses regret, and does not let the loss define her - the growth-mindset pattern. Bernard Loiseau and the Martins sort to column a because for them failure redefines the person permanently. McEnroe's headset excuse and the students reviewing worse test papers sort to column c because both repair self-esteem through blame or downward comparison rather than through learning.

assets.topic: Feeling Smart: Flawless Now vs. Learning Over Time
assets.visual_frame_description: Ms. Alvarez's fifth-grade classroom is finishing a set of challenging math puzzles. In one corner, six students are captured in thought bubbles as they answer the question, "When do you feel smart?" Amara, a girl with her hand raised mid-answer, is outlined in gold as the target of the task. Each student's spoken line floats above their head in a labeled bubble the player can tap to classify.
assets.player_mission: Classify each student's answer about when they feel smart into one of three categories: feeling smart from being flawless right now, feeling smart from learning over time, or feeling smart from being special and better than others. Sort all six answers into the correct columns.
key_concepts: When Dweck asked people when they feel smart, those with the fixed mindset said "It's when I don't make any mistakes."
Fixed-mindset people said they felt smart "When I finish something fast and it's perfect."
Fixed-mindset people also said they felt smart "When something is easy for me, but other people can't do it."
Growth-mindset people said they felt smart "When it's really hard, and I try really hard, and I can do something I couldn't do before."
Growth-mindset people felt smart when they worked on something a long time and started to figure it out.
For the growth mindset it is not about immediate perfection but about confronting a challenge and making progress over time.
In the fixed mindset you have to be pretty much flawless, and you have to be flawless right away.
People with the fixed mindset described feeling smart as times they felt like a special person, different from and better than other people.
The difference between the mindsets shows up from grade schoolers to young adults when they are asked when they feel smart.
When the fixed-mindset person asks "If you're somebody when you're successful, what are you when you're unsuccessful?", the fragility behind the self-esteem is revealed.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests what the two mindsets define as feeling smart: the fixed mindset requires flawless performance right now and superiority over others, while the growth mindset defines intelligence as learning something over time through effort. Dweck found striking, consistent differences in how people from grade school to young adulthood answered the same question.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Amara, the highlighted student, says, "When it's really hard, and I try really hard, and I can do something I couldn't do before." Which column best classifies Amara's answer?
assets.column_a_label: Feeling smart = being flawless right now (fixed mindset)
assets.column_b_label: Feeling smart = learning over time (growth mindset)
assets.column_c_label: Feeling smart = being better than other people (fixed mindset)

rows.label: "When I don't make any mistakes."
"When it's really hard, and I try really hard, and I can do something I couldn't do before."
"When something is easy for me, but other people can't do it."
"When I finish something fast and it's perfect."
"When I work on something a long time and I start to figure it out."
"When I feel like a special person, someone different from and better than other people."

distractors: Column a - feeling smart means Amara made no mistakes and finished perfectly and fast.
Column c - Amara feels smart because the puzzle made her feel more special than her classmates.
Amara's answer cannot be classified because it reflects a temporary mood rather than a mindset.
assets.explanation: Amara describes stretching against difficulty and making new progress, which is exactly the growth-mindset definition of feeling smart. The answers about not making mistakes and finishing fast and perfect sort to column a, because they demand immediate flawlessness. The answers about doing something easy that others cannot do, or feeling like a special person, sort to column c, because they hinge on superiority over other people.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Effort: A Threat or an Igniter
assets.visual_frame_description: A violin studio at Juilliard, late afternoon. Nadia, a former child prodigy now in her late teens, sits in a chair with no violin case in sight while her teacher stands by an open music stand with a bow in hand. Around the room, ghosted vignettes illustrate other attitudes toward effort: a tortoise and a hare on a finish line, a prodigy sweating through a competition rehearsal, and a professor working late in a lit office building. The player's cursor hovers over labeled evidence cards.
assets.player_mission: Study how each person in the scene treats effort and sort each evidence card into the column that names the belief behind it: effort signals low ability, effort ignites ability into accomplishment, or effort robs you of your excuses. Classify all six cards correctly.
key_concepts: People with the fixed mindset tell you, "If you have to work at something, you must not be good at it."
In the fixed mindset, effort is for people who don't have the ability; things come easily to people who are true geniuses.
The tortoise-and-hare fable and stories like The Little Engine That Could gave effort a bad name, reinforcing the image that effort is for plodders who lack endowment.
People with the growth mindset believe that even geniuses have to work hard, and that no matter what your ability is, effort is what ignites that ability and turns it into accomplishment.
Nadja Salerno-Sonnenberg, a violin prodigy with a crisis of confidence, was afraid of trying because real effort would leave her without excuses.
"Nothing is harder than saying, 'I gave it my all and it wasn't good enough'" - the deepest fear within the fixed mindset.
Dweck realized that "I could have been Yo-Yo Ma" is a claim people can only make if they never really tried.
The fixed mindset makes effort terrifying partly because great geniuses are not supposed to need it, so needing it casts a shadow on your ability.
When Salerno-Sonnenberg finally trained all-out for a competition under Dorothy DeLay, she won it.
Effort can be feared in relationships too: Amanda kept choosing unreliable boyfriends because she could not risk really trying with a genuinely good partner and having it fail.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the mindset-dependent meaning of effort: the fixed mindset reads effort as a sign of low ability and as a threat that destroys the "I could have been" excuse, while the growth mindset treats effort as the force that ignites ability into accomplishment. Dweck grounds this in the fear that paralyzed violinist Nadja Salerno-Sonnenberg and in the culture's reverence for effortless genius.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: Nadia, the highlighted prodigy, has stopped bringing her violin to lessons and refuses to fix her awkward fingerings and bowings. Which column best names the belief driving her refusal?
assets.column_b_label: Effort ignites ability into accomplishment (growth mindset)
assets.column_c_label: Effort robs you of your excuses (fixed mindset)

rows.label: Nadia refuses to correct her bowing and fingerings because changing them would admit her habits were wrong.
Nadia admits, "If you go to an audition and don't really try, if you're not really prepared, you have an excuse."
The fable of the tortoise and the hare reinforces that effort is for plodders, not for the talented.
Dweck's colleagues working late at the University of Illinois struck her as "not as smart as I am" instead of more hardworking.
"Even geniuses have to work hard for their achievements... effort is what ignites that ability and turns it into accomplishment."
Once Salerno-Sonnenberg began training all-out for a competition, she won it - and said you have to work hardest for the things you love most.

distractors: Column a - Nadia is simply lazy and unwilling to practice, regardless of what it would mean.
Column b - Nadia is wisely conserving her energy for the music she truly loves.
Nadia's refusal is best explained by her temperament, not by any belief about effort.
assets.explanation: Nadia's own words reveal the excuse-robbery mechanism: if she does not really try, she keeps the out of "I could have been." Column a captures the belief that needing effort proves you lack talent, which is what makes the fingerings so hard to change; column c captures the even sharper fear that honest effort destroys all excuses. The tortoise-and-hare lesson and Dweck's late-night colleagues sort to column a, while the quotes about effort igniting ability and Salerno-Sonnenberg's winning competition sort to column b.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: An admissions advising office at a large university. A wall-mounted screen cycles through six cases: a four-year-old at a puzzle table, Hong Kong freshmen registering for classes, a seventh-grade girl raising her hand, a pre-med student hunched over a chemistry textbook, a teenage golfer on a PGA fairway, and a cabdriver listening to opera. A counselor points at the golfer's case, which is outlined in gold as the target the player must classify.
assets.player_mission: For each case on the screen, decide whether the person's choice reflects a fixed mindset, a growth mindset, or a factor other than mindset such as temperament or resources. Sort all six evidence cards into the correct columns.
key_concepts: Four-year-olds with the fixed mindset chose to redo an easy jigsaw puzzle rather than try a harder one, because kids who are born smart "don't do mistakes."
Growth-minded four-year-olds found the choice strange and chose one hard puzzle after another; one girl said "I'm dying to figure them out!"
At the University of Hong Kong, freshmen who were not fluent in English and had a fixed mindset were not very interested in a faculty-offered remedial English course.
The Hong Kong students with the growth mindset said an emphatic yes to the remedial English course, seizing the chance to learn.
The seventh-grade girl raised her hand even when unsure of the answer so her mistakes could be corrected and she could increase her intelligence.
In Dweck's brain-wave lab at Columbia, only people with the growth mindset paid close attention to information that could help them learn.
Fixed-mindset pre-med students showed a big drop in interest as chemistry got harder; growth-mindset students kept the same high level of interest, and challenge and interest went hand in hand.
Fifth graders with the growth mindset wanted to take the hard puzzles home, and one asked the researcher to write down the names so his mom could buy more.
Michelle Wie entered the Sony Open against the best male golfers to prepare for the future, saying the learning experience was what she was after.
After the Sony Open, Wie's confidence had not suffered one bit: "I think I learned that I can play here."
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests how the two mindsets drive challenge-seeking: the fixed mindset avoids challenges that might expose deficiency, while the growth mindset actively seizes challenges as opportunities to stretch. Dweck demonstrates this across jigsaw puzzles, remedial English courses, pre-med chemistry, and a teenage golfer entering a PGA tournament.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: The highlighted case is Michelle Wie, the teenage golfer who entered the Sony Open against the best male professionals. Which column best classifies her choice?
assets.column_b_label: Growth mindset - seize the chance to stretch and learn
assets.column_c_label: Neither - temperament or resources explain it

rows.label: A four-year-old with the fixed mindset chooses to redo the easy jigsaw puzzle instead of attempting a harder one.
Hong Kong freshmen who lack English fluency decline a faculty course that would improve their English skills.
The seventh-grade girl raises her hand even when unsure so her mistakes can be corrected and she can get smarter.
Growth-minded pre-med students keep their high interest in chemistry even when the exams stay very hard.
Michelle Wie enters the Sony Open against the world's best male golfers, seeking a learning experience rather than a protected win.
A cabdriver spent years trying to cultivate a love of opera because his father loved it, and finally accepts that he never will.

distractors: Column a - Wie was avoiding a real challenge by choosing easier opponents in junior tournaments.
Column c - Wie's choice is fully explained by her fearless temperament, not by any mindset.
Column b only applies to academic settings, never to sports.
assets.explanation: Wie chose the hardest possible field not to protect her record but to learn what playing at that level felt like, and her confidence survived the loss - a growth-mindset choice. The easy-puzzle choice and the Hong Kong students' refusal sort to column a because they protect against exposing deficiency. The cabdriver case sorts to column c because Dweck treats his acceptance of not loving opera as a legitimate limit of taste and temperament, not a mindset failure.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A glass-walled boardroom in a downtown office tower. A wall of screens shows six corporate leaders in portrait: a CEO repeating the same car design, a turnaround artist waving at a soaring stock chart, an executive apologizing into a telephone, an engineer under a lamp overhauling a tech giant, a paper-company chief standing at a mill, and a disgraced energy boss pointing at the world outside the window. The player must classify each leader's strategy.
assets.player_mission: Review each corporate case on the boardroom wall and classify the strategy as protecting the hero image, confronting shortcomings for long-term growth, or assigning blame outward after failure. Sort every case into the correct column.
key_concepts: "CEO disease" describes leaders who create a world where they have no shortcomings by surrounding themselves with worshipers and exiling critics.
Lee Iacocca, after his early success at Chrysler, kept bringing out the same car models with only superficial changes and quickly lost touch with where his field was going.
Albert Dunlap, a self-professed fixed mindsetter at Sunbeam, chose the short-term strategy of looking like a hero to Wall Street; the stock soared and the company fell apart.
Lou Gerstner, an avowed growth mindsetter at IBM, accepted stagnant stock and Wall Street sneers while overhauling IBM's culture and policies, and years later IBM led its field again.
Darwin Smith, looking back on his extraordinary performance at Kimberly-Clark, declared, "I never stopped trying to be qualified for the job."
Jack Welch chose GE executives on the basis of "runway," their capacity for growth.
NASA rejected applicants with pure histories of success and instead selected people who had significant failures and bounced back from them.
Jeffrey Skilling insisted that Enron's failure was the world's fault and dismissed the Justice Department investigation into corporate deception as a witch hunt.
After the Kidder, Peabody scandal, Jack Welch phoned fourteen of his top colleagues to apologize personally, saying "I blamed myself for the disaster."
In the fixed mindset people are always in danger of being measured by a failure, and it can define them in a permanent way.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests how mindsets shape leadership: the fixed mindset pushes executives toward "CEO disease" - protecting the perfect image and choosing short-term heroics - while the growth mindset lets leaders confront shortcomings and invest in long-term development. Dweck contrasts Iacocca and Dunlap with Gerstner, Smith, and Welch, and contrasts Skilling's outward blame with Welch's personal responsibility.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.question: The highlighted case is Albert Dunlap at Sunbeam, who chose a strategy to make himself look like a hero to Wall Street. Which column best classifies his strategy?
assets.column_a_label: Protect the hero image - CEO disease (fixed mindset)
assets.column_b_label: Confront shortcomings for long-term growth (growth mindset)
assets.column_c_label: Assign blame outward after failure (fixed mindset)

rows.label: Lee Iacocca keeps releasing the same car models with superficial changes while surrounding himself with worshipers and exiling critics.
Albert Dunlap chooses a short-term strategy at Sunbeam: the stock soars but the company falls apart.
Lou Gerstner overhauls IBM's culture while stock prices stagnate and Wall Street sneers, then IBM leads its field again.
Darwin Smith of Kimberly-Clark says, "I never stopped trying to be qualified for the job."
Jeffrey Skilling insists Enron's failure was the world's fault and calls the Justice Department investigation a witch hunt.
Jack Welch apologizes personally to fourteen GE colleagues after the Kidder, Peabody scandal, saying "I blamed myself for the disaster."

distractors: Column b - Dunlap was investing in the long-term foundation of the company for its health and growth.
Column c - Dunlap blamed regulators and short sellers for the company's collapse.
Dunlap's strategy is best explained by his industry's temperament, not by his mindset.
assets.explanation: Dunlap chose the short-term strategy of looking like a hero to Wall Street, the same image-protecting pattern as Iacocca's worshipers-and-critics world, so he sorts to column a. Gerstner, Smith, and Welch sort to column b because they confronted shortcomings and worked for long-term development even under criticism. Skilling sorts to column c because he blamed the world rather than taking responsibility, in direct contrast to Welch's personal apology.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: Reframing Failure After a Lost Pitch
assets.visual_frame_description: A design studio called Lumina, mid-morning. Priya, a senior product designer, sits across from her account lead Maya at a long table covered in sticky notes and a rejected pitch deck. Maya is slumped back, arms crossed, scrolling a phone showing the rival agency's announcement. Sunlight cuts across the room; a whiteboard behind them reads "Next client: April."
assets.player_mission: Guide Priya through the conversation with Maya, who lost a major pitch and is spiraling. Choose the responses that help Maya treat the loss as an event to learn from rather than a verdict on her identity, and that steer her away from blame and downward comparison.
key_concepts: In the fixed mindset, failure shifts from an action ("I failed") to an identity ("I am a failure").
In the growth mindset, failure is a painful but nondestructive problem to be faced, dealt with, and learned from.
Seventh graders with the growth mindset said they would study harder for the next test after a poor grade.
Seventh graders with the fixed mindset said they would study less and seriously consider cheating, reasoning that without ability effort is wasted.
College students in the fixed mindset repaired their self-esteem after a bad test by looking at the tests of people who did far worse.
People with the fixed mindset may assign blame or make excuses instead of repairing the actual deficiency.
John Wooden said you are not a failure until you start to blame, because you can still learn from mistakes until you deny them.
A growth-mindset lawyer spent seven years fighting a bank on behalf of cheated clients, lost, and said he did not regret it because the effort itself was valid.
The growth mindset allows people to value what they are doing regardless of the outcome.
People with the fixed mindset may try to repair their self-esteem by going looking for people who are even worse off than they are.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the mindset-dependent response to failure: the fixed mindset turns a lost pitch into proof of a permanent flaw and reaches for blame or downward comparison, while the growth mindset treats it as a problem to study and learn from. Dweck shows fixed-mindset students repairing self-esteem through cheating, blame, and comparing with worse-off others instead of repairing the skill.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Maya Chen and Priya are senior product designers at Lumina, a mid-sized design studio. They just lost a six-week pitch for a major health-tech client to a rival agency. A week later, Maya is still devastated: she keeps rehashing the loss, muttering that the client's committee "never understands good design," saying the loss "proves I was never really senior material," and comparing herself favorably to a junior colleague named Tomas who is struggling. Priya, who wants to win the next pitch and keep Maya's morale intact, must help Maya shift out of the spiral. Stakes: Maya's confidence, the studio's next opportunity, and the health of the team.
dialogue: Maya: I can't believe it. Twelve weeks of work and they picked the other team. I feel like I've been exposed as a fraud.
Priya: You've been sitting with this all week. What's the story you're telling yourself about what this means?
Maya: It means I'm not the designer I thought I was. Everyone in the studio knows it now.
Priya: Do you actually believe one lost pitch measures who you are as a designer?
Maya: Maybe not. But it's easier to say the client's committee is clueless. And honestly, at least I'm not floundering like Tomas.
Priya: Tomas is working through his own learning curve. Comparing yourself to his struggles isn't going to make you a better designer.
Maya: So what am I supposed to do?
Priya: Let's take the pitch apart. What did we learn about how they evaluate, and what would we do differently next time?
Maya: ...You're right. I'd rather lose the excuse than the lesson.
choices: You're one of the best designers I know. Don't let one setback shake that - you have nothing to prove to anyone.
Let's book a client debrief, pull the competitor's deck, and map what we'd change. This loss is data for the next pitch.
Honestly, the committee was biased from the start. It's not fair to blame yourself.
Maybe design isn't the right field for you if a loss hits this hard.
assets.theoretical_principle: Failure as an event to be faced and learned from (growth mindset) versus failure as a verdict on fixed identity with self-esteem repaired through blame or downward comparison.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 1 works because it reframes the loss from identity to problem and turns it into a learning plan, exactly how the growth-mindset seventh graders responded by studying harder and how the growth-minded lawyer valued the validity of his effort. Choice 0 is talent reassurance that feeds the fixed mindset's ego without teaching anything. Choice 2 is outward blame, the McEnroe-style self-esteem repair that short-circuits learning. Choice 3 delivers the identity verdict - "you are a failure" - which is precisely the meaning the fixed mindset attaches to a setback.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: The 'Yet' Moment for a New Hire
assets.visual_frame_description: A bright corner office at a boutique investment firm. Rosa, a managing director, sits across from Devon, a new financial analyst who joined two weeks ago. Devon's desk across the hall is stacked with deal memos and valuation templates; he looks pale and keeps glancing at a senior analyst's finished report pinned to the wall. Rosa has just put down her coffee to lean in and listen.
assets.player_mission: Play Rosa, the new analyst's manager, and steer the conversation so Devon sees that his current inability is a state of "not yet" rather than a permanent verdict. Choose the response that gives him a concrete path to learn while holding the job's real standards.
key_concepts: Columbia graduate students with stellar records and test scores felt like complete imposters within a day, looking at the faculty and thinking "Oh my God, I can't do that."
The new graduate students knew how to take tests and get A's, but they did not know how to do the research work - yet - and they forgot the yet.
School (and a job) is there to teach; people are there to learn how to do these things, not because they already know everything.
People with the fixed mindset expect ability to show up on its own, before any learning takes place.
"Becoming is better than being," and the fixed mindset does not allow people the luxury of becoming; they have to already be.
Janet Cooke and Stephen Glass were talented young reporters who fabricated stories, possibly because they felt they should already be big-time reporters before doing the hard work of learning how.
Stephen Glass wrote, "We were stars - precocious stars - and that was what mattered."
An assessment at one point in time has little value for understanding someone's ability, let alone their future potential.
In the growth mindset, you don't always need confidence: you can plunge into something wholeheartedly even when you think you're not good at it.
Dweck says people can change mindsets just by knowing about the two mindsets and catching themselves in the fixed mindset.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the "yet": the fixed mindset reads current inability as a permanent verdict on talent, while the growth mindset treats skills as developable through learning. Dweck describes Columbia graduate students who "forgot the yet" within one day, reading their unfamiliar research demands as proof of inadequacy.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Devon, 24, is a new financial analyst at a boutique investment firm. He aced every test in college, had near-perfect grades, and was aggressively recruited, but two weeks into the job he freezes: senior analysts draft deal memos, run valuation models, and write investment committee notes he cannot yet produce. He tells his manager, Rosa, that he must have fooled everyone in the interview. Rosa knows this is the classic "yet" moment and wants to keep a talented analyst from spiraling into imposter thinking. Stakes: Devon's development, the quality of the work he will soon own, and the team's trust in the hiring decision.
dialogue: Devon: Honestly, Rosa, I think I got this job by mistake. Everyone here writes memos in their sleep and I can't even start one.
Rosa: You've been here two weeks. What exactly can't you do yet?
Devon: Everything that matters. I don't know how to value a deal, I don't know the models, and I'm not like the others.
Rosa: Were you like the others on day one? Nobody walks in knowing this. You know how to take tests and get A's - you just don't know this yet.
Devon: But my grades and my interview answers were all I had. If I can't do the work, it means I never really had the talent.
Rosa: Or it means you're in a room full of people who've practiced for years. The talent got you here; the practice carries you from here.
Devon: So you're not going to write me off?
Rosa: I'm going to pair you with Dana on the next deal memo and give you the model templates. Your job is to ask every question you have. That's how you learn.
choices: Don't worry about it, Devon. You were hired for a reason - you're clearly brilliant. Just be patient.
You're not ready yet - and that's why you're here. Here's the deal memo template; work through it with Dana and bring me your questions.
I need to be honest: if you can't keep up by Friday, we'll need to reconsider the fit.
Feeling like an imposter means you don't belong here. Maybe you should have taken that offer from the other firm.
assets.theoretical_principle: The "yet": the fixed mindset treats current inability as a permanent verdict on talent, while the growth mindset treats skills as developable and learning as the very purpose of the role.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 1 names the missing yet, reframes the gap as a learning stage, and gives Devon a concrete structure, matching Dweck's point that people are hired to learn how, not because they already know everything. Choice 0 is empty talent praise that reinforces the fixed mindset and leaves Devon with no skill-building plan. Choice 2 turns a one-point-in-time assessment into a threat, the fixed mindset's "a test score is forever" logic. Choice 3 confirms the imposter verdict and drives him out.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A polished dance studio with mirrored walls and a barre. Ms. Alvarez, the director of a competitive youth ballet program, stands beside Elena, a 17-year-old dancer who has just finished a fouetté sequence. A few younger students watch from the floor, and Elena's expression hardens the moment Ms. Alvarez opens a notebook that contains her corrections. The scene is quiet except for the sound of a metronome app on a phone.
assets.player_mission: Play Ms. Alvarez in a conversation with Elena, a gifted student who thrives on praise but wilts under correction. Choose the response that teaches Elena to treat correction as information for growth rather than proof she lacks talent, and decide how to run the rehearsal accordingly.
key_concepts: Marina Semyonova, a great Russian dancer and teacher, made students survive a trial period while she watched how they reacted to praise and to correction.
Semyonova's students had to be more responsive to correction to be deemed worthy - she separated those who get their thrill from what's easy from those who get their thrill from what's hard.
"This is hard. This is fun" was the moment Dweck knew she was changing mindsets.
In the fixed mindset it is not enough to succeed - you have to be pretty much flawless, and you have to be flawless right away.
Fixed-mindset people said they feel smart when they don't make any mistakes and when they finish something fast and perfect.
Growth-mindset people said they feel smart when they work on something a long time and start to figure it out.
Even the best puzzle-solvers among fifth graders showed a plunge in enjoyment when the puzzles got harder, so puzzle talent did not prevent the decline.
The self-esteem movement encourages people to confirm their superiority, as with the "I LOVE ME" mirror, instead of building their skills.
Effort is what ignites ability and turns it into accomplishment, no matter what your ability is.
In the fixed mindset, needing effort casts a shadow on your ability, because great geniuses are not supposed to need it.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the Semyonova principle: response to correction, not response to praise, reveals which mindset a learner has and which learners will grow. Dweck recounts how Marina Semyonova selected students by watching whether they got their thrill from what was easy or from what was hard, and how the fixed mindset requires flawless performance right now.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Ms. Alvarez runs a competitive youth ballet program with a demanding performance season ahead. Elena, 17, is her most naturally gifted dancer, but she only absorbs praise: any correction makes her sulk, withdraw, and threaten to quit. Elena's parents press Ms. Alvarez to praise her constantly to protect her confidence. Ms. Alvarez knows the program's culture is at stake and wants to model how a growth-minded studio treats correction. Stakes: Elena's development, the example she sets for younger students, and the quality of the season's company.
dialogue: Elena: Did you see my fouettés today? Everyone said they were perfect.
Ms. Alvarez: I saw them. Now let's talk about the extension in your arabesque - it collapsed on the landing.
Elena: (turns away) Fine. I guess I'm just not cut out for this.
Ms. Alvarez: Why does a correction make you want to quit?
Elena: Because if I was actually talented, I wouldn't need to be fixed all the time.
Ms. Alvarez: Here's the truth about this studio. I don't pick dancers who are already perfect. I pick dancers who get energized by correction.
Elena: That's backwards. Everyone else praises me.
Ms. Alvarez: Praise tells you where you already are. Correction tells you where you could go. Which one is going to make you the dancer you want to be?
Elena: ...Nobody's ever said it like that. So what do I work on first?
choices: You're the most naturally gifted dancer here, Elena. Don't let one correction shake your confidence.
From now on I'll only critique the students who ask for it. You just keep dancing and enjoy it.
Let's start with the arabesque. Here's the drill - you'll be off balance for a week, and that's exactly what growing feels like. I'm watching your process, not your perfection.
If corrections make you this upset, maybe competitive dance isn't for you.
assets.theoretical_principle: Marina Semyonova's selection test: separate students who get their thrill from the easy from those who get their thrill from the hard, judging them by their response to correction rather than to praise.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 2 reframes correction as the path of growth, demands engagement with the hard part, and makes process visible, which is exactly how a growth-minded teacher selects for learners. Choice 0 is talent praise that keeps Elena's confidence contingent on never being wrong. Choice 1 removes the challenge and protects her ego at the cost of development. Choice 3 delivers the fixed-mindset identity verdict, confirming her fear that correction means she is not cut out for dance.

assets.topic: Choosing a Partner: Pedestal or Growth
assets.visual_frame_description: A café on a rainy Saturday afternoon. Lena, a 29-year-old event planner, wraps both hands around a mug across from her friend Sam. A wedding invitation lies on the table between them. Lena looks tired and keeps glancing at her phone, which shows a string of missed calls from Marcus. The screen displays Sam's and Lena's thoughts as the conversation unfolds.
assets.player_mission: Play Sam, Lena's trusted friend, as she describes a boyfriend who adores her but crumbles at any criticism. Choose the advice that helps Lena see what she actually wants from a partner - someone who fosters her development rather than a worshiper who needs her to be flawless.
key_concepts: People with the fixed mindset said their ideal mate would put them on a pedestal, make them feel perfect, and worship them.
People with the growth mindset hoped for a partner who would see their faults and help them to work on them.
Growth-minded people wanted someone who would challenge them to become a better person and encourage them to learn new things.
Growth-minded people did not want people who would pick on them or undermine their self-esteem, but they did want people who would foster their development.
A growth-mindset woman told of her marriage to a fixed-mindset man who was devastated by any request and then ran to his mother for the constant adoration he needed.
The fixed-mindset husband's idea of success - total, uncritical acceptance - was not the wife's, and her idea - confronting problems - was not his.
One person's growth can be the other person's nightmare when the mindsets clash.
People with the growth mindset did not assume they were fully evolved, flawless beings who had nothing more to learn.
In the fixed mindset, if you're somebody when you're successful, what are you when you're unsuccessful?
The self-esteem movement invents devices like the "I LOVE ME" mirror to help people confirm their superiority instead of fostering development.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the ideal-mate question: the fixed mindset wants a partner who enshrines fixed qualities through pedestals and worship, while the growth mindset wants a partner who challenges and fosters development. Dweck's young-adult surveys showed these two sharply different pictures of the ideal mate, and a fixed-mindset partner's need for uncritical adoration can make one person's growth the other's nightmare.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: Lena, 29, an event planner, has been dating Marcus for five months. Marcus showers her with compliments and cancels his own plans for her, but he collapses at the smallest criticism. When Lena asked him to consult her before booking weekend plans, he was devastated, then spent an hour on the phone with his mother so she could reassure him he was wonderful. Lena is wondering whether she is being too picky and asks her friend Sam for a read on the relationship. Stakes: Lena's judgment about what a good relationship actually is.
dialogue: Lena: I feel like I have to walk on eggshells. I asked Marcus to run weekend plans by me, and he acted like I'd insulted him to his core.
Sam: What happened after that?
Lena: I spent an hour rebuilding his mood, and then he called his mom so she could tell him he's wonderful. We never even talked about my actual request.
Sam: What do you want a partner for - to feel perfect, or to grow?
Lena: I want someone who sees my faults and helps me work on them. Who challenges me to be better. Not a cheerleader for everything I do.
Sam: Then Marcus is giving you the opposite of what you want. He needs total, uncritical acceptance.
Lena: Is that really so bad? He adores me.
Sam: Adoration that breaks the second you disagree isn't adoration. It's a pedestal, and it doesn't foster development.
Lena: So I should end it?
Sam: I can't answer that. But ask yourself: does this relationship make you grow, or does it exist to make you feel flawless?
choices: Marcus sounds great. Someone who worships you is what everyone really wants - don't overthink it.
Ask yourself what you're actually getting here. You want a partner who fosters your development; he wants a relationship where nobody raises an issue. Those two things don't coexist.
You're the problem, Lena. You're too sensitive - most people would love being adored.
Dump him immediately. Anyone who calls his mother that often is a red flag.
assets.theoretical_principle: The ideal-mate question: fixed-mindset people seek a partner who enshrines their fixed qualities, while growth-mindset people seek a partner who fosters their development and challenges them to become better.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 1 holds Lena's own stated values (development, challenge, working on faults) up against what Marcus needs (uncritical adoration), letting her see the mismatch herself - the growth-minded picture of a partner. Choice 0 validates the pedestal and the fixed mindset's idea of love. Choice 2 turns the critique onto Lena's identity, the fixed-mindset verdict. Choice 3 is an outcome verdict that skips the deeper question about what fosters growth.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A shared grad-student apartment in late February; gray light through the window, a pile of unopened mail, and a lecture hall timetable stuck to the fridge. Priya sits on the edge of Jonah's bed while he stays under a blanket, laptop open to a blank document. A three-week calendar on the wall is dotted with X marks over missed deadlines, and a sticky note reads "Lab hours: Mon-Sat."
assets.player_mission: Play Priya, Jonah's roommate, as he sinks into a depressive slump. Choose the responses that help him keep his life intact by staying in motion, even while feeling wretched, instead of letting the setbacks define him or letting everything slide.
key_concepts: In Dweck's three-week online diary study during February and March, students with the fixed mindset had higher levels of depression.
Fixed-mindset depression came from rumination: tormenting themselves with the idea that setbacks meant they were incompetent or unworthy.
The more depressed fixed-mindset students felt, the more they let things go and the less they took action to solve their problems.
Plenty of students with the growth mindset felt miserable in peak depression season, but the more depressed they felt, the more they took action to confront their problems.
Growth-minded students, when depressed, made sure to keep up with their schoolwork and their lives.
A depressed freshman kept going to class and doing the reading; his teaching assistant told him, "then you're not depressed."
He was depressed, but he was coping the way people in the growth mindset tend to cope - with determination.
Temperament certainly plays a role in how people react, but mindset is an important part of the story.
When Dweck's team taught people the growth mindset, it changed the way they reacted to their depressed mood.
When people believe in fixed traits, they are always in danger of being measured by a failure that can define them permanently.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests mindset and depression: fixed-mindset students who felt depressed ruminated on setbacks as evidence of incompetence and let everything slide, while growth-minded students, the more depressed they felt, took more action and kept up their lives. Dweck found that teaching people the growth mindset changed how they reacted to a depressed mood, independent of temperament.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.scenario_setup: It is late February, the peak of the campus depression season. Priya's roommate Jonah, a first-year graduate student, has been sliding for three weeks: he sleeps till noon, has stopped going to lab, missed two assignment deadlines, and keeps muttering that the setbacks prove he is not cut out for grad school. Priya worries that letting everything slide is the fixed-mindset pattern she learned about in her psych seminar. Stakes: Jonah's semester and mental health, and the routines that would keep his life intact until he feels better.
dialogue: Jonah: I'm a dope. I failed that midterm, and now the paper's late and I can barely get out of bed. This just keeps circling: I'm not cut out for grad school.
Priya: You've been beating yourself up for two weeks. What's the story you're holding onto?
Jonah: That the last two weeks prove I'm worthless. What's the point of trying?
Priya: In my psych seminar we talked about this - people who see setbacks as evidence they're broken tend to let everything slide. People who see them as problems keep their routine.
Jonah: So I should pretend I'm fine?
Priya: No. You're not fine. But you can be wretched and still shower, go to lab, and turn things in - so that when you feel better, your life is still intact.
Jonah: That sounds like a lot of effort for nothing.
Priya: The worse you feel, the more determined you get - that's the research finding. Drag yourself in tomorrow, and I'll sit with you while you write the first draft.
Jonah: ...Okay. Meet me at the lab at nine.
choices: You're clearly depressed. Take a break from everything - your assignments can wait until you feel better.
I get it, you're a dope, I felt that way last semester too. You'll be fine in a few weeks.
You're not a failure - you're just sensitive by temperament, and some people can't handle this kind of pressure.
Keep the routine anyway. Shower, show up, hand things in, even if you feel awful - when you feel better your life will still be intact. I'll go with you.
assets.theoretical_principle: Mindset and depression: fixed-mindset students who felt depressed ruminated on setbacks as proof of incompetence and let everything slide, while growth-minded students, the more depressed they felt, took more action and kept up their lives.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 3 matches the growth-mindset coping style Dweck documented: feeling wretched but still showing up, so that life remains intact when the mood lifts. Choice 0 is the fixed-mindset slide - letting things go because the setback feels like a verdict. Choice 1 labels Jonah with an identity verdict and offers empty reassurance. Choice 2 writes the whole thing off to temperament, which Dweck says plays a role but is not the whole story, since teaching the growth mindset changed people's reaction to a depressed mood.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: The city desk of a metro newspaper, late evening. A young reporter named Eric, 26, types furiously at a terminal while a stack of front-page stories sits beside him. His editor leans over a printout with a red marker circling one detail. On the wall, framed front pages show the paper's best work, and in the corner a veteran reporter watches Eric with concern. The scene glows with the tension of a deadline.
assets.player_mission: Study Eric's behavior and diagnose the mechanism driving it, then choose the intervention that holds him accountable while refusing to treat one mistake as a permanent verdict on his identity. Defeat the 'prove-it-right-now' urgency before it destroys a talented career.
key_concepts: Janet Cooke won a Pulitzer Prize for Washington Post articles about an eight-year-old drug addict, but the boy did not exist and she was stripped of the prize.
Stephen Glass was the whiz kid of The New Republic whose stories and sources turned out not to exist.
Dweck understands them as talented, desperate young people who succumbed to the pressures of the fixed mindset.
Stephen Glass wrote, "We were stars - precocious stars - and that was what mattered."
"Becoming is better than being," and the fixed mindset does not allow people the luxury of becoming; they have to already be.
People with the fixed mindset expect ability to show up on its own, before any learning takes place.
In the fixed mindset one test or one evaluation can measure you forever, which is why success must be perfect and immediate.
School and the workplace are there to teach; people are there to learn how to do these things, not because they already know everything.
In the fixed mindset failure shifts from an action to an identity: "I am a failure."
People with the fixed mindset may repair self-esteem after a failure through blame and excuses rather than by repairing the skill.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the 'prove-it-right-now' urgency: in the fixed mindset, one evaluation can measure you forever, so success must be flawless and immediate, and admitting ignorance feels like disqualification. Dweck reads the fabrications of Janet Cooke and Stephen Glass through this lens - talented young people who felt they had to already be big-time reporters before doing the hard work of learning how.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central mechanism is the fixed-mindset urgency to be flawless right away: if one evaluation can measure you forever, then every correction or moment of not-knowing feels like proof of permanent inadequacy, pushing a person to fake success rather than learn. This battle tests whether you can spot that urgency behind a rising reporter's fabrications and replace it with a learning orientation before it costs him his career.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are the city editor of a metro newspaper. A new reporter, Eric, 26, has delivered three splashy front-page stories in six weeks - unusually fast for a rookie. You notice he panics whenever anyone asks for a source's phone number, changes details under questioning, and has started calling older reporters to check how real journalists handle pushback. Yesterday you asked him to rewrite a small corrections note and he looked physically ill. You study a scene of high talent combined with terror: a young man who behaves as if admitting ignorance would discredit him, who feels he must already be a big-time reporter before doing the hard work of learning how.
assets.stage_1_question: Which mechanism best explains Eric's pattern of behavior?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The fixed-mindset urgency to be flawless right away: Eric reads any correction or request for a source as evidence that he is not truly talented, so instead of learning he performs success - the same pressure Dweck sees behind Janet Cooke's fabricated Pulitzer-winning story and Stephen Glass's invented sources at The New Republic, where feeling he had to already be a star outweighed doing the hard work of learning how.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You catch one embellished detail before it reaches print: a quote Eric attributed to a source who never said it. The publisher wants to fire him immediately, and the union representative wants you to issue a public reprimand. Before anyone acts, you pull Eric aside. He finally admits, in a low voice, "I can't be seen learning on the job." You have one move that sets the culture of the newsroom. How do you respond?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Hold Eric accountable for the fabrication as a behavior to correct while refusing to frame him as a permanent failure: walk him through exactly what he did wrong, reassign him for a month to a veteran reporter's beat where learning on the job is the explicit and normal expectation, and praise his corrections and process rather than his splash. This mirrors the growth mindset's treatment of a mistake as something to be faced, dealt with, and learned from, and it treats "not yet" as a stage rather than a verdict. Firing him or publicly shaming him would confirm the fixed-mindset belief that one failure defines him forever - the exact belief that drove the fabrication.

assets.domain: Growth vs. Fixed Mindset | Attribution Theory
assets.topic: The Fear of Effort in a Star Performer
assets.visual_frame_description: An engineering team's open office at sprint planning. Theo, 31, a celebrated coder who wrote his first app at twelve, leans back with his chair tipped, arms behind his head, telling the team he "could have built the new payment system in a weekend if he'd wanted to." Around him, teammates exchange glances, and a whiteboard lists the sprint's stories with Theo's name next to a row of question marks. The manager watches from the doorway.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose the fear driving Theo's pattern of never committing fully, then choose an intervention that makes real effort the explicit and safe expectation. Defeat the 'I could have been' shield before it lets a star performer coast into mediocrity.
key_concepts: Nadja Salerno-Sonnenberg, a violin prodigy, was paralyzed by fear of trying and had stopped bringing her violin to her lessons.
She said everything she was going through boiled down to fear: "Fear of trying and failing."
Without effort you can always say "I could have been..."; once you really try, you can't say that anymore.
"Nothing is harder than saying, 'I gave it my all and it wasn't good enough'" - the deepest fear within the fixed mindset.
Dorothy DeLay confronted the prodigy: "If you don't bring your violin next week, I'm throwing you out of my class."
When Salerno-Sonnenberg finally trained all-out for a competition, she won it.
"You have to work hardest for the things you love most" is something Salerno-Sonnenberg says she knows for a fact.
In the fixed mindset, great geniuses are not supposed to need effort, so just needing it casts a shadow on your ability.
Fear of effort can happen in relationships too: Amanda kept choosing unreliable boyfriends because she could not risk genuinely trying with a good partner and having it fail.
High effort is a big risk when your claim to fame is having no deficiencies, because effort can reduce you.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the fear of effort in the fixed mindset: needing to try casts a shadow on talent, and actually trying robs a person of the "I could have been" excuse, so the highest-stakes risk is an honest failure. Dweck traces this fear through violin prodigy Nadja Salerno-Sonnenberg and shows how a confrontation that demanded real effort - Dorothy DeLay's ultimatum - freed her to win.

credibility.basis: Empirical education psychology (Dweck's mindset research; replication nuance)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central mechanism is the fixed mindset's fear of effort: because geniuses are not supposed to need effort, trying casts a shadow on your ability, and because a real attempt leaves no excuses, an honest failure is the scariest possible outcome. This battle tests whether you can see that fear behind a talented employee's self-sabotage and intervene so he actually puts in effort instead of preserving his excuses.
assets.stage_1_observation: You manage a team of software engineers. Theo, 31, is a coding prodigy who has been called a genius his whole career. But he dodges every high-stakes project: he forgets the sprint planning meeting, turns in partial work, and always has an excuse ready - "the ticket was ambiguous," "my machine kept crashing," "the deadline was unrealistic." He has never actually failed, because he has never actually tried. In this morning's stand-up he bragged that he could have built the new payment system in a weekend if he'd wanted to. You watch a very talented man who is terrified of an honest failure.
assets.stage_1_question: Which mechanism best explains Theo's pattern?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Fear of effort and honest failure: Theo protects his "natural genius" identity by never committing fully, so any setback can be blamed on circumstance rather than ability - the fixed-mindset logic that trying and still failing is the worst possible outcome because it leaves no excuses, the same fear that stopped Nadja Salerno-Sonnenberg from bringing her violin to class.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You assign Theo the new payment system project - the one he bragged he could do in a weekend. It is a six-week build. On day three he turns in a skeleton that does not compile and says he "had other priorities." His mentor suggests you reassign him to easy tickets to keep his confidence intact. You pull Theo into your office. What do you do?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Refuse to reassign him, and make real effort the explicit, safe expectation: tell Theo the project is his, that you expect him to work hard on it, that struggling is a normal part of the job, and that you will measure him on what he learns and how he improves rather than on flawless genius - then meet weekly to review his process. This mirrors Dorothy DeLay's confrontation of Salerno-Sonnenberg, which demanded genuine effort and led to her winning the competition, and it treats "working hardest for the things you love" as a virtue. Reassigning him to easy tickets would confirm the fixed-mindset bargain that effort signals low ability and that his excuses must be preserved.
